pillars.building: Complete the module's labs (Expectation, variance, and the √n standard error: predict the spread, then measure it shrink; Bayes and the base rate: predict 1/6, then simulate a million people; Maximum likelihood: predict `p̂ = k/n`, then confirm it by calculus and by grid) and the module assessment.

tiers.materialGround: A distribution is a list of outcomes with non-negative weights that sum to 1. Expectation is their weighted average, `Σxᵢpᵢ`, and is linear unconditionally — `E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]` even for dependent variables. Variance is `E[(X−μ)²] = E[X²]−μ²`; it adds only for independent variables, and the mean of `n` independent draws has variance `σ²/n`, so its standard error shrinks like `σ/√n` — quadruple the data to halve the error. Conditional probability is restriction-then-renormalization, `P(A|B)=P(A∧B)/P(B)`, and Bayes' rule makes the posterior `P(A|B)` depend on the prior/base-rate `P(A)`; a 99%-accurate test for a 1%-prevalence disease yields a posterior of exactly `1/6`. Maximum likelihood reads a distribution formula backwards — data fixed, parameter free — and the MLE of a Bernoulli rate is `k/n`, of a Gaussian mean the sample average, of a Gaussian variance the mean squared deviation (`/n`). Every one of these you derived by hand *and corroborated by seeded simulation* this module. These are among the least contestable facts in the entire AI stack — a simulation of a million draws either confirms your formula or exposes your bug, and there is no arguing with it. **Tier 2 — what the mathematical dressing suppresses.** Every one of those clean results sits on assumptions the notation makes invisible, and probability's dressing is uniquely good at lending false authority. *The `σ/√n` standard error assumes independent, identically distributed draws* — but real data is correlated (the same user rated ten movies, the same site served a thousand requests), correlated draws carry *less* information than `n` independent ones, and the honest standard error is *larger* than `σ/√n` — so the naive formula **overstates confidence**, always in the reassuring direction. *A posterior is only as trustworthy as its prior*, and "prior" spans a range from a measured base rate (defensible) to a number someone picked (a value judgment wearing a probability's clothes); the formula processes both identically and reports the same crisp posterior, so a contestable assumption exits the equation dressed as a fact. *A likelihood is maximized under a model you chose* — "the MLE" is the best parameter *assuming the data really is Bernoulli / Gaussian*, and when the model is wrong the MLE is confidently, precisely wrong. The equation never lies; it answers *exactly* the question you encoded — the iid you assumed, the prior you fed, the family you chose — which is rarely exactly the question you meant. Boosters say "the model learned the probability"; critics say "it's just curve-fitting to assumptions" — both dodge that the assumptions are *load-bearing and often unverifiable*, and no amount of math can referee whether your draws were really independent or your prior really justified. **Tier 3 — sit with this.** Your model ships a probability with every decision: a `0.94` that this transaction is fraud, this applicant will default, this scan is malignant. tiers.materialGround: A loss landscape is a scalar-valued function of parameters, nothing more exotic than the `f(x,y)` you have been differentiating since M03. Convexity is a checkable property (chord above curve; Hessian positive semi-definite) that, when present, guarantees any local minimum is the global one and that gradient descent with a small enough learning rate finds it. Gradient descent's stability is bounded, per direction, by `η < 2/λᵢ` for each Hessian eigenvalue `λᵢ`, and the worst direction sets the ceiling for the whole trajectory. A minibatch gradient, properly sampled, is an unbiased estimator of the full gradient with variance that falls as `1/m` — both facts you verified by exhaustively enumerating and averaging every possible batch, not by taking anyone's word for it. Saddle points, not bad local minima, dominate the critical points of high-dimensional nonconvex landscapes. None of this is a matter of opinion; every claim in this paragraph was hand-computed and then measured to agree, in this module's labs. **Tier 2 — what the mathematical dressing suppresses.** "The model converged" sounds like a discovery — an objective, checkable fact about the world. Lesson 4 showed exactly what it actually claims: an update size or gradient norm fell under a threshold, at whichever point a particular random seed, minibatch order, and learning-rate schedule happened to land the trajectory. Two runs of the identical architecture on identical data, differing only in random seed, can both "converge," both report similarly low validation loss, and land at two genuinely different points in a nonconvex landscape — different basins, like the double well's `+1` and `−1`, potentially with different behavior on inputs neither training run happened to emphasize. The word "converged" carries none of that contingency; it reads as a terminus, a settled fact, when what actually happened was one particular trajectory's arrival at one particular, arbitrary-among-many-similar point. A learning-rate schedule, a batch size, an early-stopping patience counter — each is a value-laden choice about how much noise to tolerate and how early to trust a flat gradient, rendered invisible the moment a training run prints a single scalar loss and a boolean. Boosters say "the model was trained until convergence," which sounds like rigor; critics say "it just stopped when the numbers looked good enough," which sounds like nothing was decided. Both dodge the load-bearing fact: **convergence is a claim about where an algorithm's particular walk happened to stop, not a claim about the walk having found the best place to be — and the difference between those two claims is exactly the difference this module spent eighteen hours teaching you to check.** **Tier 3 — sit with this.** Your team trains the same architecture on the same data three times, differing only in random seed. All three runs "converge" — gradient norm below threshold, loss curves that look, by eye, identical. All three land in different regions of a nonconvex parameter space, the way this module's double well sends two hairs'-width-apart starting points to opposite basins. On your validation set, all three score within a rounding error of each other. You ship one of them. Nothing about the number you reported — the final validation loss — reveals that the other two exist, or that they might behave differently from the one you shipped on the exact input that later goes wrong for someone. tiers.materialGround: Entropy `H(p) = −Σ pᵢ log pᵢ` is the expected surprisal of a distribution and, by Shannon's source coding theorem, the provable minimum average number of bits (or nats) needed to encode outcomes drawn from it — not a metaphor, a bound you can watch real compressors approach. Cross-entropy `H(p,q) = −Σ pᵢ log qᵢ` is the average cost of encoding true data `p` with a code shaped for guess `q`, and for a one-hot label it collapses to `−log q_true` — exactly the loss `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` reports. KL divergence `D_KL(p‖q) = H(p,q) − H(p)` is the extra cost that mismatch causes, is provably `≥ 0` (Gibbs' inequality) with equality only at `p=q`, and is provably asymmetric — `D_KL(p‖q) ≠ D_KL(q‖p)` in general, a fact you verified with two different numbers on the same pair of distributions. Because `H(p)` is fixed by the data and does not depend on model parameters, minimizing cross-entropy loss during training is algebraically identical to minimizing KL divergence to the true data distribution, which is algebraically identical to maximizing likelihood. These are chained, provable facts, not a stack of loosely related tools — you derived each link in the chain by hand, and every one of them you verified numerically against a finite difference or a random-sampling property test, the least contestable layer of the whole AI stack. **Tier 2 — what the mathematical dressing suppresses.** Cross-entropy is a single scalar, and that is exactly its danger: `−(1/N) Σ log q_{true}` is an *average*, and an average is a number that has already decided which errors to erase. A model can drive its training loss beautifully low while being catastrophically, confidently wrong on a thin slice of the distribution — a rare disease, a minority dialect, an edge-case fraud pattern — because that slice contributes a handful of large terms to a sum over millions, and the sum does not preserve the shape of where the badness lives. The loss curve going down is real evidence the model is fitting *something*; it is not evidence about *what* it might still be getting wrong, or for whom. Worse: cross-entropy is minimized against whatever `p` you handed it — the labels — and the formula has no mechanism to notice if `p` itself encodes a biased sampling process or an unrepresentative labeling standard. A model trained to convergence on biased labels achieves a genuinely, mathematically low cross-entropy loss; the arithmetic is flawless and says nothing about whether the labels were fair. Boosters point at "the loss converged" as evidence of learning; critics point at "it's just curve-fitting to whatever data you fed it" as evidence of nothing. Both dodge the same fact: **the loss faithfully measures agreement with the distribution you chose to call ground truth, and the choice of that distribution is not inside the mathematics — it is a decision you made before the first gradient step, and the loss cannot audit it for you.** **Tier 3 — sit with this.** Your model's training log reports a cross-entropy loss of `0.31` — low, respectable, the kind of number that gets a model shipped. Nothing in the number `0.31` distinguishes these two worlds. An auditor asks you a question this module has given you the exact tools to answer honestly: not "what was your average loss," but "show me the cross-entropy, per example, sorted from worst to best — and tell me who is in the tail." tiers.materialGround: A complexity class converts to a wall-clock and memory bill, and you can compute the bill on your own laptop. At 1 ns/operation, an O(N²) algorithm costs ~17 minutes at a million items and ~32 years at a billion — a slope, not a constant, and no affordable hardware closes that gap. Append is O(1) *amortized* because doubling the backing array bounds total copies below 2N (a geometric series), while growing by one slot costs N(N−1)/2 copies — O(N²) total — and both bounds are exact, checkable with the copy-counting array in Lab M01-B. The doubling test recovers an unknown function's class from the ratio T(2N)/T(N) because the constant cancels. A Python list of distinct ints costs ~36 bytes/element, so a 16 GB machine hits its memory wall at N ≈ 4×10^8 — it cannot reach 10^9 by *bytes*, independent of speed. All of this is measured with `time`, `timeit`, and `sys.getsizeof`, which ship with the interpreter. It is documented, not opinion.
tiers.observerReading: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil" and "just make it work first" are true advice that quietly hides a second truth: **the complexity class is not an optimization, it is a design decision made before the first line runs**, and getting it wrong is not something you "optimize later" — it is something you *rewrite*, often after it has already failed someone in production. The booster culture that says "scale is a good problem to have, worry about it when you get there" cannot admit that O(N²) doesn't degrade gracefully — it works fine in the demo at N=1000 and becomes physically impossible at N=10^9, with no warning in between. The performance-purist counter-culture cannot admit that below the crossover, the "worse" algorithm is genuinely correct and their instinct to reach for the asymptotically-optimal structure wastes real effort. Both are half true. Big-O is neither a premature optimization to defer nor a purity test to pass — it is a *budget you either priced or didn't*, and the field's two loudest camps each have a reason not to say so.
tiers.sitWithThis: Every "efficient" system draws a budget line — a latency SLA, a memory ceiling, an index that fits in RAM — and everything on the wrong side of that line is *dropped*, not served slowly. When your retrieval index is fast because it's approximate, the speed is bought by *not finding* the hardest-to-find items: the rare document, the underrepresented name, the query that doesn't cluster near anything. The budget didn't fail — it worked exactly as designed, and the cost landed entirely on whoever sat past the line you couldn't afford to cross. So: when you choose a complexity class, you are choosing an N you will serve and an N at which the thing falls over — and *someone is always at the N you decided not to reach.* Whose retrieval did your budget silently decide wasn't worth the bytes? And will you ever see their name, given that the whole point of the budget was to never scan far enough to find it?

tiers.materialGround: A hash table computes a slot from a key instead of searching for it: `index = hash(key) & (capacity − 1)`, one arithmetic op and one array load, and *that* is the source of "O(1)." Every claim in this module is checkable at the keyboard. `hash(42) == 42` and `hash(-1) == -2` in CPython; a `list` of a million ints and an `int64` NumPy array of the same values sum with identical O(N) slope but a ~30× constant gap you can measure; a from-scratch open-addressed table that deletes with EMPTY *will* fail to find a colliding key after a middle delete, and a tombstone *will* fix it, both demonstrable in five lines; a `dict` built from objects whose `__hash__` returns a constant builds in Θ(n²) — double n, quadruple the time — while remaining perfectly *correct*, every key present with the right value. And CPython's string-hash randomization is real: `python3 -c "print(hash('x'))"` prints a different number each process. None of this is opinion; all of it is a measured slope or a printed value. **Tier 2 — What the field suppresses.** Two opposite distortions hide the same truth. The booster distortion — "hash tables are O(1), use a dict and move on" — suppresses that the O(1) is an **average over a uniformity assumption**, and averages have distributions. "O(1) average" is compatible with *some specific keys* costing O(n): the keys that collide, the keys an adversary chose, the keys whose `__hash__` you wrote carelessly. The cost did not disappear; it got **redistributed onto whichever keys the hash fails to spread**, and the aggregate stayed cheap precisely because the expensive cases are rare — rare, not absent, and not randomly assigned. The traditionalist distortion — hashing as a solved, boring primitive, collisions as a textbook footnote — suppresses that collision behavior is a live *security and fairness* surface: hash flooding was a real cross-language CVE, string randomization is a mitigation with a known hole (integers and custom hashes are undefended), and the "average" that makes the structure fast is an average *someone's* keys sit at the bad tail of. Both camps avoid the honest middle: **a hash table is fast on average by being slow on a minority, and which minority is not decided by the structure — it is decided by the hash function and by who supplies the keys.** **Tier 3 — Sit with this (a question you cannot unknow).** You will build systems that hash people. Deduplication that hashes names and birthdates to decide who is "the same person"; caches keyed by user ID; feature stores, join keys, blocked-record matching — all of it leaning on the same bet, that the hash spreads the keys so the average stays O(1). But the average is bought by a tail, and the tail is not random: it is the keys that collide, the values that repeat, the names that are common, the records that don't fit the shape the hash was tuned for. The person whose lookup is the slow one, the record that lands in the over-full bucket, the identity that collides with someone else's and gets silently merged — **when you report your system's latency as a single average number and it passes every correctness test, whose O(n) did you fold into everyone else's O(1), and would you be able to name them — or has the structure, by design, made the person paying the cost the one you are least able to see?**

units.title: Trees, heaps, and top-k at scale
units.summary: The first module where the driving *operation* — **top-k**, "give me the k best out of N" — is the thing retrieval and ranking actually run millions of times a day, and we descend beneath `sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:k]` to the structure that makes it affordable at 10^9. We build a binary heap by hand (an array wearing a tree costume), implement top-k **two ways**, and predict — before measuring — which one wins at large N and small k, and *why the answer changes* when you swap pure Python for a C-accelerated call or push N past the memory wall.

tiers.materialGround: A binary heap is an array with three index formulas; `push`/`pop` walk one root-to-leaf path, so both are O(log N) — at most 19 swaps at a million items, 29 at a billion, measurable with the copy/swap-counting heap in Lab M03-A. `heapify` builds a heap in O(N), not O(N log N), because the per-node work sums as `N·Σ h/2^h = N·2` — a convergent series, checkable by timing `heapify` against N repeated pushes. Top-k has two exact implementations: sort-then-slice (O(N log N) time, O(N) memory) and the bounded min-heap (O(N log k) time, O(k) memory, streaming), and Lab M03-B proves they return *identical* results. At N = 10^7, k = 10 the pure-Python bounded heap (~12 s) is *slower* than C `sorted` (~5 s) despite the better Big-O — the interpreter tax (~50×/op) beats the 9× operation savings — while `heapq.nlargest` (~1.4 s, the same algorithm in C) wins; all three timed with `timeit`. A Python float costs ~32 bytes/element, so `sorted` on 10^9 floats needs ~32 GB and cannot run on a 16 GB machine, where the streaming heap holds a few hundred bytes — measured with `tracemalloc` in Lab M03-C. All of it runs on a laptop with stdlib + NumPy.
tiers.observerReading: "Just use `heapq.nlargest`, top-k is a solved one-liner" is true and hides two things the reversal exposes. First, the booster framing — *"the better algorithm is the one with the better Big-O"* — cannot admit that at real-world N in a real language the **constant decides**, and that the "obviously better" O(N log k) heap loses to the "worse" O(N log N) sort until you also pay off the interpreter tax; complexity class is necessary and *not sufficient*, and the field teaches only the necessary half. Second, and deeper: the whole framing of top-k as "return the k best" treats *"best"* as a solved, neutral quantity — as if the scores were handed down objectively and the only engineering question is retrieving the top of them cheaply. But the score is a *model's* judgment, and top-k is a **hard cutoff**: item k is served and item k+1 is discarded, with no gradient between them, on the strength of a score difference that may be noise. The performance-purist counter-culture, obsessed with shaving the constant, cannot admit that the *fastest* correct top-k and the *fairest* selection are different problems and optimizing the first does nothing for the second. Both camps optimize the retrieval and neither audits the ranking that the retrieval faithfully, efficiently, serves.
tiers.sitWithThis: Every top-k draws a line at rank k and discards everything below it — that is the operation, exactly as designed and now, having built it, exactly as you understand it. When the k best are *exact* (your bounded heap), the line is at least honest: item k+1 really did score below item k. But production doesn't stay exact — it goes *approximate* (M05's ANN index, AIE-302's RAG) to reach the N where exact top-k can't fit, and approximation doesn't shave the line evenly. It prunes whole regions of the candidate space *without scanning them*, and the items in those unscanned regions — the document unlike any cluster, the name that embeds far from every neighbor, the query that matches nothing closely — are dropped not because they scored below k but because the fast index *never compared them at all*. The heap you built returns the true top-k of what it sees; the system it lives in decides what it sees, and buys its speed by not looking everywhere. So: when you return "the top 10," you are asserting a completeness you did not verify — that the best 10 were among the candidates the index bothered to score. Whose result was never in the heap because the fast path pruned the region they live in? And since the entire point of the speed was to *not scan that far*, what would it even take for you to notice they were missing — or is "efficient retrieval" precisely the name we give to never having to find out?

units.title: Graphs: traversal, shortest paths, PageRank intuition
units.summary: The module where the structure under every knowledge base, link graph, and citation network stops being a diagram and becomes code you traverse by hand. A "relationship" — cites, links-to, is-similar-to, calls — is an edge; a knowledge base is a graph before it is anything else. We build the graph as the substrate M02 already gave us (a dict is an adjacency list), walk it two ways (BFS, DFS), find shortest weighted paths by re-using the M03 heap, and then ask the question that turns a graph into a ranking: not "is X connected to Y" but "how *important* is X," answered not by counting links but by an eigenvector — a bridge over the water to AIE-103's linear algebra, crossed here on foot before you're handed the boat.

tiers.materialGround: A graph is nodes plus edges; the adjacency list, built on a Python dict (M02's hash table), costs O(V+E) memory against the adjacency matrix's O(V²) — at V=10^6 that gap is measured directly: a few hundred MB versus 8 TB for the identical information, and by V=10^8 the matrix's 10^16 cells are not representable on any machine. BFS and DFS are both O(V+E), verified by direct traversal of a 6-node worked graph (BFS: `A,B,C,D,E,F`; DFS: `A,B,D,E,C,F`, both reproducible with `test_graph.py`); a recursive DFS provably crashes with `RecursionError` on a 2000-node chain (Python's default recursion limit is 1000) while an iterative version completes. Dijkstra, built on M03's `MinHeap`, computes exact shortest weighted paths (`test_dijkstra.py`'s worked example: `A→C→B` at cost 2 beats the direct `A→B` at cost 4); measured on random-weight graphs, the heap-based version beats a naive array-scan by 25.5× when sparse and remains at least as fast (1.12× margin) even at 99.9% density, because realized relaxation counts (measured: 2,851 pushes against 632,847 possible edges on an 800-node dense graph) track close to `V log V`, far below the `E`-driven worst-case bound. PageRank, computed by power iteration on the transition matrix, converges to the same answer as direct eigen-decomposition (`np.linalg.eig`, agreeing to 4 decimal places) in 24–47 rounds at O(E) per round, while `eig` costs O(V³) and O(V²) memory — measured 91×–428× slower across V=200–900, and requiring 80 GB at V=10^5, past the 16 GB wall. All of it — the pricing tables, the traversal traces, the Dijkstra race, the PageRank convergence — runs on a laptop with stdlib + NumPy.
tiers.observerReading: "PageRank ranks by importance" is the one-sentence version everyone learns, and it hides two things the module's own mechanics expose. First, the booster framing treats "importance" as a property the algorithm *discovers*, when the worked example shows precisely what it *computes*: a recursive function of who already links to you, weighted by who links to them. A brand-new, genuinely important paper or page has, by construction, few or no inbound links yet — PageRank cannot distinguish "not yet linked because it's new" from "not linked because it's unimportant," because the algorithm has no notion of time, only structure. It rewards *accumulated* endorsement, and calls the result "importance" — a category error the field mostly declines to name, because "importance" sells better than "accumulated-endorsement-so-far." Second, and more structural: the entire computation — BFS, Dijkstra, PageRank — operates *only* on the graph as given. A node that was never linked to is not a low-ranked node in the graph; it **is not in the graph**. There is no "rank zero" bucket for the unlinked — they are absent from V entirely, which means every pricing table, every traversal, every convergence guarantee in this module is scoped to "the part of the world someone thought to link." The performance-purist counter-culture, fixated on making Dijkstra and power iteration faster, has nothing to say about this — speed is orthogonal to completeness, and neither camp treats "who got left out of V" as an engineering question, though it plainly is one: it's a decision made by *whoever chose which edges to crawl or record*, upstream of any algorithm in this module.
tiers.sitWithThis: You built the traversal and the ranking; you know exactly what each one computes. BFS finds the truly shortest path *among nodes in the graph*. Dijkstra finds the truly cheapest path *among edges you recorded*. PageRank computes the mathematically correct dominant eigenvector *of the matrix you built*. Every one of these guarantees is airtight — conditional on `V` and `E` being complete. But `V` and `E` are never complete; they are *whatever got crawled, cited, linked, or logged* — and the module's own PageRank example already showed that being linked from an important node matters far more than being linked from many unimportant ones, which means a node's absence from a *few* well-connected sources' link lists — a citation index that stopped tracking a smaller journal, a hyperlink crawler that never found a site behind an unusual URL scheme, a knowledge graph built from a corpus that skipped a language — doesn't just lower that node's rank. It can erase it, because a node with **zero** recorded in-links isn't ranked low by PageRank; it may not be a node in your graph at all. So: your graph doesn't fail to rank someone highly. It fails to *contain* them, silently, upstream of every algorithm you just proved correct — and correctness is exactly what makes the omission invisible, because a correct BFS, a correct Dijkstra, a correct PageRank all return confidently, with no error, no low score, no signal that anything is missing. What would it even look like to notice that your graph is missing a node you never crawled the edge to — and whose job, in the systems you'll build after this course, is it to go looking?

units.title: Similarity search: exact to approximate nearest neighbors
units.summary: The differentiator module. Every AI system you will ever build ends in the same operation — "given this query vector, find the k most similar things out of N" — and every RAG pipeline, every recommender, every dedup system, every semantic cache calls it thousands of times a second. We descend beneath `sklearn.neighbors` and beneath every vector-database "just call `.search()`" call to the two structures actually doing the work: the flat vectorized scan (exact, and it dies), and the index built to avoid scanning at all (approximate, and it can silently fail to find someone). You build both by hand, race them, and predict — before measuring — where the exact one dies and where the approximate one's recall falls off a cliff. The index you build here (`NSWIndex`) is the ANN component **AIE-302 (RAG) imports** to select the k nearest chunks against a real corpus.

tiers.materialGround: Exact cosine-similarity search is one BLAS call, `X @ q`, O(N·d) time and O(N·d) memory — measured at 79 ms/query and 2.86 GB at N=1,000,000, d=768 on the authoring machine, and extrapolable (disclosed as extrapolation) to ~79 s/query and ~2.86 TB at N=10^9, past what a single machine can serve or hold. A 15–16 GB machine stops fitting a production-dimension (d=768) corpus around 5–6 million vectors — arithmetic reproducible with `bytes/vector = d × 4` against any machine's real RAM. Locality-sensitive hashing turns "approximate" into a computable probability — `P(collision) = (1 − θ/π)^L` per table, `1 − (1 − P)^T` across T tables — and Lab M05-C measures that the naive formula (0.967 at a realistic L,T for a 0.9-similarity pair) overstates real recall@10 (0.250, measured) because k neighbors must survive simultaneously, not just one pair. A from-scratch navigable-small-world graph (`NSWIndex`, Lab M05-B) achieves recall@10 from 0.147 to 0.980 by sweeping its beam width `ef_search`, and — measured, not asserted — loses to exact brute-force search on wall-clock at every tested setting at N=5,000, by roughly 3× to nearly 80×, because the interpreter tax on each Python-level graph hop dwarfs the operation-count savings at this N; the crossover is estimated (extrapolated from measured curves) around N≈2×10^5 at d=64. Both LSH and NSW store the *entire* corpus (`self._vectors`/`self.vectors`) plus a smaller index overhead — verified directly with `tracemalloc` — so neither reduces the memory wall the exact scan hits; they reduce query time only.
tiers.observerReading: "Vector databases scale to billions" is the field's dominant claim, and it is technically achieved — but by *bundling two separate fixes* (a sub-linear index for time, plus quantization/compression for memory) and marketing them as one, so that an engineer who reaches for "just add an ANN index" to a memory-constrained system gets a working demo at 10^5 rows and a production incident at 10^8, because the index they added never touched the axis that was actually going to break. This module's Tier 1 gives you the receipt: `NSWIndex` at N and d costs essentially the same corpus memory as brute force, full stop, a fact any vector-database vendor's marketing page omits by simply never stating what "scale to billions" is scaling *along*. Second, and this one implicates the from-scratch builder as much as the vendor: **recall@k, reported as a single averaged number, is precisely the statistic that hides who the index fails.** A system that reports "97% recall" sounds nearly exact. But recall@k averaged across a benchmark query set says nothing about the *distribution* of that failure — whether the missing 3% is spread thinly and randomly across every query, or concentrated entirely on a specific subset of queries that score near-zero every time. Both produce the identical headline number. The field ships the headline number because it's the one number that fits in a comparison table; it does not, by construction, ship the distribution, and a distribution is exactly what you'd need to know whether "97% recall" means "everyone is a little bit worse off" or "everyone is fine except this group, always."
tiers.sitWithThis: You built `NSWIndex` by hand. You know, because you measured it, that it is not exact — that its beam search can converge on a local optimum and never reach the true nearest neighbor, and that this happens more, not less, for query vectors sitting in a sparse or unusual region of the embedding space, where fewer nearby graph edges exist to route a greedy walk toward the right answer. LSH has the same shape from a different mechanism: a vector unlucky enough to land, by the accident of a few random hyperplanes, in a bucket with nothing similar to it, is simply never compared to its true neighbors — no error, no signal, just a query that returns confidently and is quietly wrong. Both failure modes concentrate on the same kind of point: the outlier, the vector unlike its neighbors, the query that sits far from every cluster your index's structure was built around — which, translated out of the geometry and into what these vectors usually *represent* in a real system, is the document unlike the corpus, the phrasing unlike the common phrasings, the name or the context that embeds far from where most embeddings cluster because it belongs to whoever is least like the majority the model was trained on. Recall@k, averaged across a benchmark, will never single this out — it reports one number, and one number cannot distinguish "everyone loses 3%" from "this person loses 100% of the time, every time, and nobody else loses at all." So: you now know how to measure recall. You do not, from that measurement alone, know *whose* queries live inside the 3% you didn't catch — and the entire economic case for building this index instead of the exact one was that you would stop checking every candidate. What would it take to find out who's inside that 3% — and if finding out requires doing the exact, expensive, exhaustive check you built this index specifically to avoid doing, was the index ever really answering the question "who is nearest," or only the cheaper question "who is nearest, among those I decided in advance to look at"?

units.title: Streaming and sketching: counting when you can't hold the data
units.summary: this is the module that builds **the streaming counter** the course arc names by name. M02 built the hash table (exact membership, O(1), but it must hold every key). M03 built the heap (the exact k best, O(k) memory, but it must still touch every element once). This module asks the question those structures cannot dodge forever: what do you do when even O(N) time to *look* at the data is fine, but O(N) **memory** to *hold* it is not — when N is a day of clickstream events, a week of log lines, a lifetime of embeddings, and no single machine will ever hold the distinct set at once? You descend beneath `x in my_set`, `len(set(stream))`, and `counter[key] += 1` to the bit array and the register file doing the arithmetic underneath, build a Bloom filter, a Count-Min sketch, and a HyperLogLog counter **by hand**, predict their error *before* you run them, and re-ascend able to choose an exact structure or a bounded-memory approximation **by a measured error budget**, not a shrug.

tiers.materialGround: Reservoir sampling (Algorithm R) produces a provably uniform sample of size k from a stream of unknown length in one pass and O(k) memory — the telescoping proof in Lesson 1 shows every stream position ends at exactly probability k/n, verified empirically in Lab M06-A. A Bloom filter is an m-bit array plus k hash functions; it has **zero false negatives, structurally** (a bit is only ever set, never cleared, by every insertion of every item that touches it) and a false-positive rate `p ≈ (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k` that is tunable at design time and measurable after the fact, confirmed to within tolerance for a 1,000,000-item, 1%-target filter in Lab M06-B. A Count-Min sketch is a `w × d` grid of counters; because every update only adds, never subtracts, `estimate(x) ≥ true_count(x)` **always**, with a magnitude bound `ε·N` from the width and a confidence bound `1-δ` from the depth, demonstrated on a hand-traced six-cell table where the minimum-across-rows recovers two of three exact counts despite two independent collisions, and confirmed at scale in Lab M06-C, where a real sketch's measured overestimate stays inside the `ε·N` bound and an isolated 100,000-count heavy hitter survives 1,000 rare-key collisions with its estimate essentially untouched. HyperLogLog estimates distinct count from the longest observed run of leading zeros in a hashed bit string, bucketed across `m = 2^b` registers to control variance, with standard error `1.04/√m` — a number that does not depend on the true cardinality, only on the memory paid — verified against a known exact count in Lab M06-D, at 768 bytes for `m=1024` versus tens of megabytes for the exact `set()` it replaces at the same scale, and a memory gap that only widens as N grows because the sketch's footprint doesn't move. **Tier 2 — what the field suppresses.** "Just use a sketch, approximate is basically free at this scale" is the booster line, and it hides two things this module's formulas make hard to unsee. First: none of these errors are *symmetric noise* the way "measurement error" sounds when the word "approximate" gets used loosely. A Bloom filter's error only ever says yes when the truth is no — never the reverse — which means whatever decision sits downstream of "is this on the list" is *structurally biased toward inclusion*, not toward a coin-flip; if that filter guards a blocklist rather than a dedup check, the bias runs exactly backwards from what a security engineer would want, and "it's only a 1% error rate" is describing the wrong shape of error to be reassuring about. Count-Min's overestimate is the same one-directional story pointed at rate limits and heavy-hitter detection: every estimate creeps upward, never downward, so a system built on it will over-report load, over-throttle, and over-flag — never under —, and "the error averages out" is not a sentence that formula supports. Second, and quieter: "1% false-positive rate" sounds small precisely because it's phrased as a percentage, and percentages hide absolute counts at the scale these structures are built for. A Bloom filter serving a billion queries a day at a 1% false-positive rate produces **ten million** wrong "yes" answers daily — small as a fraction, enormous as a headcount, and the percentage framing is doing real rhetorical work to make that headcount invisible. **Tier 3 — sit with this (a question you cannot un-ask).** Every sketch in this module buys its bounded memory by refusing to keep a receipt. A hash set that says "yes, X is a member" can, if asked, also say *why* — X is sitting right there, an entry you could point to. A Bloom filter that says "yes" cannot: the bits that triggered the answer are shared with an unknown number of other items, by design, and there is no operation that recovers which of them actually caused this particular "yes." That is not an implementation gap to be fixed in a future version — it is the entire mechanism by which the structure stays small. So: when a Bloom-filter-backed blocklist falsely flags a legitimate account because that account's hash happens to collide with a bad actor's, the block is not a one-time unlucky event — it is **deterministic and permanent**, the exact same collision, every single time that account is checked, for as long as the filter's parameters don't change. And the system has no way to discover this happened, because discovering it would require keeping the very thing the sketch was built specifically to not keep. The same shape recurs in Count-Min (whichever key's true count gets silently inflated by collision with a heavier key stays inflated, invisibly, and the sketch offers no operation to ask "was my count polluted") and in HyperLogLog (the distinct entity whose hash landed on a register that a *different* entity's hash later overwrote with a longer run is not undercounted in a way anyone can trace back to them specifically — the register just doesn't remember). Ask the question the way this module's labs made you answer it for the exam: not "is there some error," but *who, specifically, and would the system you just built even have the evidence to tell them if they asked?* If the honest answer is "no, and that's not a bug, that's the compression," what obligation does that put on you, the one person in the pipeline who understood the mechanism well enough to have predicted it — before you shipped the sketch that made the receipt impossible to produce?
